title: Functional interpretation of GWAS · Tuesday, November 24

transcript.text: This is the Paper Library daily on Functional interpretation of GWAS, for Tuesday, November 24.
Let's turn to functional interpretation of GWAS. Both papers today are resources for getting from an associated locus to a mechanism.

The first is a bioRxiv preprint from the Hitz lab describing the IGVF Catalog, a knowledge graph from the Impact of Genomic Variation on Function consortium. It integrates 657 consortium datasets, including reporter assays, CRISPR perturbation screens, coding variant assays and predictive enhancer-gene models, with public GWAS, QTL, linkage disequilibrium and annotation data.

The scale is large: nearly 3 billion nodes and more than 8.6 billion edges, which carry effect sizes, significance and biological context. You can query it through a web portal, Python and R clients, an API, and a Model Context Protocol server for language-model agents.

The case studies show how it works in practice. The authors resolve a FOXA1-dependent enhancer variant that regulates CAMK1D at a type 2 diabetes locus. They also separate a coding mechanism at GCKR from a regulatory one at HNF1A for liver traits, and link vascular elements perturbed by CRISPR interference to CDKN2A, CDKN2B and NOS3 in coronary artery disease.

Keep in mind that it's a preprint, and those are showcase loci rather than a systematic benchmark. The second paper, from the Huang lab in Nucleic Acids Research, is CellColocDB, which approaches the same problem through colocalization.

They ran coloc on 2805 GWAS covering 1201 traits against 316 bulk, sorted-cell and single-cell QTL contexts. Coloc-SuSiE and SMR with HEIDI add supporting evidence, and the top SNPs are linked to fine-mapping results from seven methods.

The release holds about 1.6 million colocalizations with a posterior probability of a shared variant of at least 0.8, searchable by disease, gene, locus or cell context. Colocalization shows a shared signal, not causality, so experimental data like IGVF's complement it well.
The takeaway is that variant-to-function evidence now comes in resources you can query, and combining colocalization with perturbation data is a practical path from loci to mechanisms.

papers.title: CellColocDB: a disease-centred resource linking GWAS loci to genes, cell contexts, and fine-mapping evidence
